situation:
You are the merchandise sales manager at the LAUREL POINT PERFORMING ARTS CENTER, a fourteen-hundred-seat hall that has presented touring theatre and music on the same downtown block for forty years. The director of operations (judge) has asked you to set the merchandise plan for next season before the buying budget is committed.

THE FOUNDRY, a venue that opened across the river two years ago, has taken a growing share of the same audience, partly by selling licensed show merchandise on the night a tour plays there. LAUREL POINT sells from one lobby kiosk with limited shelf space, and its sales staff hear the same request at every intermission: patrons ask for the title of the show they have just watched.

The cheaper plan is to stock house-brand goods printed locally with the LAUREL POINT name, which carry no license fee and the lowest cost per unit. If patrons leaving a show still want that show's title rather than the hall's, the season's whole buying budget sits in the stockroom as unsold house-brand stock, and the kiosk has no shelf space left for anything else.

The other plan is to sign licensing agreements with the touring producers for show-specific merchandise. Each title carries a license fee and a minimum order, both owed whether the run sells out or not, so a week that draws a thin house leaves the center paying fees on titles nobody bought. It also commits most of the budget before the season is even announced.

The director of operations (judge) wants a recommendation on the assortment and the licensing, and wants to hear how you would place the merchandise in the lobby for impact. The director of operations (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the director of operations (judge) at the LAUREL POINT PERFORMING ARTS CENTER. Business background is the same as the situation above.

The buying budget for next season goes out this month and the lobby kiosk has to be stocked either way. You want to hear which merchandise plan the sales manager recommends, how the kiosk would be laid out, and you want to hear as much about the plan that was set aside as about the one that was chosen.

During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: Which plan did you decide against?
What would that one have cost the center?
